Routes of Queer Flight

Eleven documented corridors mapped against UNHCR's recognised routes. Every pop-up cites a source. UNHCR does not disaggregate route-level flows by SOGIESC; the queer geography is reconstructed from NGO casework — Rainbow Railroad, ORAM, HIAS, Iraqueer, Helem and their peers — and from country-level legal documents.

Where queer people are forced to leave, the path they take to a country that will register them, and the much smaller list of countries that will let them stay — read as one continuous map, with the gap between what UN agencies count and what civil society documents made visible. The corridors below carry forced migration that is real, sustained, and largely off the published spreadsheet.

A · INTRO

All eleven corridors, at once.

The map to the right shows every documented queer displacement corridor in this dataset — eleven of them — alongside seven UNHCR-recognised routes that share geography but not the same population. Where the two overlap, the SOGIESC share is not publicly disaggregated. Scroll to walk through them, one at a time.

Each corridor is anchored by a legal driver (the statute, the ruling, the killing) and the civil-society organisations doing the casework. The pop-ups under each stop carry the citations. Section B then turns to the axes this map first missed — intersex people, sex characteristics, and the humanitarian-data gap.

Z · COVERAGE GAP

Where the data goes silent.

UNHCR's Routes Monitor (February 2026) does not disaggregate any route-level flow by SOGIESC. Where a per-cent figure appears in this map's pop-ups, it is from NGO casework — otherwise we flag it. The Philippines is intentionally absent: same-sex relations are not criminalised, and queer-specific transit through Manila is not documented in the way it is for the corridors shown.

What you have just scrolled through is the public record. The unrecorded share is, by definition, larger.

Methodology & coverage gap

Sources listed under each stop are starting points — verify the most recent version before citing. NGO casework numbers (Rainbow Railroad, ORAM, HIAS, Iraqueer, Helem, Casa Frida, Roshaniya, Equal Asia Foundation, Russian LGBT Network, Blue Diamond Society) are programmatic outputs, not statistical samples. Country statutes are cited by article number where possible. UN documents are cited by symbol (e.g. A/HRC/56/CRP.8).
Intersex / sex-characteristics layer (Section B) drawn from OII Europe's Intersex Refugees & Asylum Seekers programme: Toolkit (Luan Pertl & Jana Hugo, 2024); live programme page (updated 25.11.2025); Petra Sussner (2020), Flucht – Geschlecht – Sexualität; EUAA Asylum Report 2024 (diverse SOGIESC); UNHCR, Working with LGBTI Persons in Forced Displacement; Council of Europe Recommendation CM/Rec(2025)7 on Equal Rights for Intersex Persons (adopted 7 Oct 2025). Destination IGM-ban tiers follow OII Europe's IGM Ban Indicators / Good Practice Map and are partial, evolving and must be re-verified before citing.
Humanitarian-action layer (Section B) drawn from Outright International & Edge Effect, "They Know What We Don't: Meaningful Inclusion of LGBTIQ People in Humanitarian Action" (July 2024) — a literature review plus interviews with staff from 12 international humanitarian organisations and case studies in Colombia, Lebanon, Myanmar, Nepal and Ukraine. This layer reframes displacement as an in-crisis aid-access problem, distinct from the asylum/resettlement corridors. Colombia and Ukraine appear only in this layer; they are not among the eleven documented corridors.
Cartography: Natural Earth projection · world-atlas 110m countries (TopoJSON) · D3 v7.
Type: Big Shoulders Display, Space Grotesk, JetBrains Mono (Google Fonts).
Layers can be toggled in the filter rail; year slider hides corridors whose primary documented driver post-dates the selected year. Markers and routes are coloured by stop kind, not by route identity, so a country that is both transit (for one corridor) and destination (for another) carries the colour of its higher-tier role on this view.
Last data refresh: 2026·02 against UNHCR Routes Monitor, OHCHR thematic reports, HRW country desks, and partner NGO public reports.
